/**
 * /ai-agents: the avatar cast. One ORIGINAL character per agent family.
 *
 * These are Nxeon's own drawings, deliberately stylised. They are NOT the
 * logos or mascots of OpenClaw, xAI/Grok, Anthropic/Claude, n8n or the Model
 * Context Protocol, and must never be traced from or styled after one. The
 * real projects are only named, factually, as what each character "runs"
 * (nominative use). Official marks, when the owner adds them, live in
 * ai-agents-marks.ts and are shown BESIDE a character, never instead of it.
 *
 * Every avatar is a 160x160 inline SVG with a shared anatomy the page script
 * and CSS drive (page.css `.av-*`, page.js):
 *   .av-body    breathing (scale from the feet)
 *   .av-eyes    blinking (scaleY)
 *   .av-pupils  cursor tracking (page.js translates it, max ±3.5 units)
 *   .av-brows   expressions (raised when the character is "active")
 *   .m-idle / .m-happy   two mouths, swapped by the .is-happy state
 *   .sig-*      the character's signature motion
 * Gradients live once in the page (CAST_DEFS) so repeated avatars share them.
 * Everything animates with transform/opacity only and stops under
 * prefers-reduced-motion.
 */

export type CastId = "claw" | "visor" | "quill" | "plug" | "flow" | "bit";

export type CastMember = {
  id: CastId;
  /** the character's own name (ours) */ name: string;
  /** what it runs: the real project named nominatively */ runs: string;
  /** short, in character, no product claims */ line: string;
  /** what it does, one sentence (crew stage) */ job: string;
  /** its signature move, for the crew stage caption */ sig: string;
  /** accent colour */ acc: string;
  /** illustrative boot script for the crew stage terminal (sample, not live) */ boot: string[];
  /** illustrative chat exchange once "online" */ reply: [string, string];
  /** illustrative task it works on in the "at work" set piece */ task: string;
};

/**
 * /ai-agents: the avatar cast. One ORIGINAL character per agent family.
 *
 * These are Nxeon's own drawings, deliberately stylised. They are NOT the
 * logos or mascots of OpenClaw, xAI/Grok, Anthropic/Claude, n8n or the Model
 * Context Protocol, and must never be traced from or styled after one. The
 * real projects are only named, factually, as what each character "runs"
 * (nominative use). Official marks, when the owner adds them, live in
 * ai-agents-marks.ts and are shown BESIDE a character, never instead of it.
 *
 * Every avatar is a 160x160 inline SVG with a shared anatomy the page script
 * and CSS drive (page.css `.av-*`, page.js):
 *   .av-body    breathing (scale from the feet)
 *   .av-eyes    blinking (scaleY)
 *   .av-pupils  cursor tracking (page.js translates it, max ±3.5 units)
 *   .av-brows   expressions (raised when the character is "active")
 *   .m-idle / .m-happy   two mouths, swapped by the .is-happy state
 *   .sig-*      the character's signature motion
 * Gradients live once in the page (CAST_DEFS) so repeated avatars share them.
 * Everything animates with transform/opacity only and stops under
 * prefers-reduced-motion.
 */

export type CastId = "claw" | "visor" | "quill" | "plug" | "flow" | "bit";

export type CastMember = {
  id: CastId;
  /** the character's own name (ours) */ name: string;
  /** what it runs: the real project named nominatively */ runs: string;
  /** short, in character, no product claims */ line: string;
  /** what it does, one sentence (crew stage) */ job: string;
  /** its signature move, for the crew stage caption */ sig: string;
  /** accent colour */ acc: string;
  /** illustrative boot script for the crew stage terminal (sample, not live) */ boot: string[];
  /** illustrative chat exchange once "online" */ reply: [string, string];
  /** illustrative task it works on in the "at work" set piece */ task: string;
};

  {

07FAQ
Straight answers.

    
Is there a one-click OpenClaw image?
Not yet. Today you deploy a clean Ubuntu server and run OpenClaw's official installer, which takes a few minutes. A hardened one-click template is coming soon, and we'll only say it exists once it does.

    
Does the server include the AI model or API credits?
No. Nxeon provides the server. Model usage, whether that's xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI or another company, is billed by that company under your own account. Running a large model locally needs far more memory than these plans have.

    
How much RAM does an agent need?
A chat bot that calls a hosted model is light: {{nxm:size_starter}} is plenty. OpenClaw or n8n are more comfortable on {{nxm:size_standard}}. Browser automation uses a lot of memory, so start at {{nxm:size_pro}}. You can resize later.

    
Is it safe to run an agent that executes commands?
Run it in its own VM, not on your laptop or next to production. Keep its control panel off the public internet, open only the ports you need, treat third-party skills and plugins as untrusted code, and snapshot before you add one.

    
Can my agent create and manage its own server?
Partly. Today an API key can list your servers, and /llms.txt describes our plans. Creating servers, scoped tokens, an MCP server and per-token budgets are planned and marked "coming soon" above.

    
Is the "at work" animation real data?
No. The tasks, clock, activity feed and counter are an illustrated sample showing how agents can run in parallel on one server. They aren't measurements of anything.

    
Are you affiliated with OpenClaw, xAI, Anthropic or n8n?
No. We name these projects only to describe software you can run on your own server. The names are trademarks of their owners, and the characters on this page are our own drawings, not their logos or mascots.

07FAQ
Straight answers.

    
Is there a one-click OpenClaw image?
Not yet. Today you deploy a clean Ubuntu server and run OpenClaw's official installer, which takes a few minutes. A hardened one-click template is coming soon, and we'll only say it exists once it does.

    
Does the server include the AI model or API credits?
No. Nxeon provides the server. Model usage, whether that's xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI or another company, is billed by that company under your own account. Running a large model locally needs far more memory than these plans have.

    
How much RAM does an agent need?
A chat bot that calls a hosted model is light: {{nxm:size_starter}} is plenty. OpenClaw or n8n are more comfortable on {{nxm:size_standard}}. Browser automation uses a lot of memory, so start at {{nxm:size_pro}}. You can resize later.

    
Is it safe to run an agent that executes commands?
Run it in its own VM, not on your laptop or next to production. Keep its control panel off the public internet, open only the ports you need, treat third-party skills and plugins as untrusted code, and snapshot before you add one.

    
Can my agent create and manage its own server?
Partly. Today an API key can list your servers, and /llms.txt describes our plans. Creating servers, scoped tokens, an MCP server and per-token budgets are planned and marked "coming soon" above.

    
Is the "at work" animation real data?
No. The tasks, clock, activity feed and counter are an illustrated sample showing how agents can run in parallel on one server. They aren't measurements of anything.

    
Are you affiliated with OpenClaw, xAI, Anthropic or n8n?
No. We name these projects only to describe software you can run on your own server. The names are trademarks of their owners, and the characters on this page are our own drawings, not their logos or mascots.

A chat bot that calls a hosted model is light: {{nxm:size_starter}} is plenty. OpenClaw or n8n are more comfortable on {{nxm:size_standard}}. Browser automation uses a lot of memory, so start at {{nxm:size_pro}}. You can resize later.

Is it safe to run an agent that executes commands?

Run it in its own VM, not on your laptop or next to production. Keep its control panel off the public internet, open only the ports you need, treat third-party skills and plugins as untrusted code, and snapshot before you add one.

Can my agent create and manage its own server?

Partly. Today an API key can list your servers, and /llms.txt describes our plans. Creating servers, scoped tokens, an MCP server and per-token budgets are planned and marked "coming soon" above.

Is the "night shift" animation real data?

No. The tasks, clock, activity feed and counter are an illustrated sample showing how agents can run in parallel on one server. They aren't measurements of anything.

Are you affiliated with OpenClaw, xAI, Anthropic or n8n?

No. We name these projects only to describe software you can run on your own server. The names are trademarks of their owners, and the characters on this page are our own drawings, not their logos or mascots.

I'm building the perspective floor grid, background server racks with LED-like gradients, blurred aurora blobs that slowly rotate, glowing ellipse platforms beneath the front characters, and a cursor-reactive light using a translated radial gradient layer rather than paint-heavy background-position changes.

I'm also setting up the staggered entrance choreography with per-word and per-character animation delays using custom properties, making sure everything stays visible and static under reduced-motion settings.

For the kinetic h2 reveal-on-scroll, I need to guard against JS failing to add the visible-state class, so I'm scoping the hidden state behind an `.ag-js` flag set early by page.js rather than risking a flash of hidden content if scripts don't load — since the h2 sits below the fold, this timing is safe. I'm also planning idle avatar animations like breathing, blinking, and occasional signature gestures on long cycles, with offscreen pausing to save performance.

Now I'm laying out the "work" set piece: a relative box with desktop aspect ratio, an absolute SVG network overlay, a centered core/server image, and six agent positions arranged around it at specific percentage coordinates. Each agent gets an avatar plus a task card beside it, and I'm sketching out the sizing math at a 1440px viewport to make sure the top-row agents near the header bar have enough room.

I'm reworking the layout so the agent block is wider and shorter (avatar left, card right) and moving the top/bottom row positions to 22%/78% to avoid overlapping the header beats/clock and the bottom ticker/count bar -- which I'll instead place outside the box in normal flow above and below, keeping the box itself as just the stage. Now I'm thinking about the center server image with a task queue stacked beneath it.

Task cards get animated via a flying element created at the queue's center that moves to each agent's position using coordinates from getBoundingClientRect, then fades out. I'm planning out the beat choreography for the ~9s loop: queue chips stacking in with staggered pop-ins and clock advancement, then a dispatch phase where chips fly to each agent with staggered timing and trigger working states and intensified packet effects, followed by a work phase where progress bars fill at varying durations per agent along with scrolling logs and ring animations, and finally a completion phase triggering burst particles as each bar finishes.

After each agent completes I want LED indicators to turn green, ticker items to update, counters to increment, and the mascot to show a happy expression; once everything's done there's a brief pause before resetting state and looping, with the clock advancing roughly 2 hours per cycle and a night overlay whose opacity responds to the time. For pausing, I need to stop the scheduling flag, pause CSS animations, pause SVG animations, and pause any WAAPI animations via the Animation API. The ticker is a capped list of 4 items with slide-in entrances and removal of older entries, and the ring indicator uses a dashed circular border that rotates while the agent is actively working.

Once a task is done, the ring should switch to solid green with a pulse scale effect. I'm now planning the crew stage layout as a three-column grid — a vertical tab list on the left, a centered podium with a spotlight cone and glowing base, and an info panel on the right — with avatars stacked and transitioning in/out based on selection, plus a happy state once chat is answered. Since custom properties can't transition smoothly without being registered via @property, and that registration risks being broken by scoping or hoisting issues in this setup, I'm deciding to skip it and just snap the color change with a brief radial pulse overlay instead. For the story section, I'm computing scroll progress to drive a chapter index, then using chapter-based CSS classes with transitions to animate different visual states as the user scrolls.

Setting up per-chapter progress variables so the server, idea bubble, crew, and night scene elements each fade, scale, or translate smoothly based on their own clamped 0-1 progress value...

input.message:
## /ai-agents v2: rebuilt as a living agent world, with the night-shift set piece and brand-mark slots

The page is rebuilt from scratch on branch `feature/ai-agents-hosting` (worktree `/tank/nxeon-wt-agents`) as commit `f9a8724ba1`, on top of v1 `1a559d91e7`. It is not merged and not deployed, and the live site is untouched. `tsc --noEmit` has 0 errors. The full test suite has 43 failures, the same set as clean `main` (I compared the lists). The page's own test passes 7/7.

### What changed
- **Hero is now a scene.**
  - The six original characters are drawn at a new 160px scale and appear roughly 3–4 times bigger on screen (claw about 300px wide at 1440).
  - They live in a parallax rack world around the owner's server-stack art, with an aurora background, a perspective floor, particles and a light that follows the cursor.
  - Each one has eyes that track the cursor, blinking, breathing, happy/active expressions and its own signature motion:
    - Pinch snaps and scuttles.
    - Vex scans, with jets.
    - Quill types, and a thought bubble appears.
    - Socket plugs a cable into a port (spark, LED turns green).
    - Nodi juggles nodes.
    - Bit runs a boot sequence.
  - On load, the headline rises word by word and the characters drop in. This is CSS-only, so there is no flash before the script runs.
- **"The night shift" set piece (your intense parallel-work request).** Six agents work at once on one server in four beats: Queue, Dispatch, Work, Done.
  - Task cards fly out from a queue: reply to a chat, scrape and summarise, deploy a site, answer a webhook, run a nightly job, triage an inbox.
  - While they work, progress bars fill, dashed rings spin, logs stream and lights flip from amber to green. Background code-glyph columns and data packets run along glowing paths routed from the real layout.
  - Each finish triggers a particle burst and adds a line to the activity feed. A counter goes up and a day-to-night clock and sky advance.
  - It is labelled on the page as an illustrative sample that is "not live data or a measure of real throughput", and the FAQ repeats that.
  - It has its own Pause button, pauses when off screen, and nothing flashes faster than 3 times a second.
- **Meet the crew is now interactive.**
  - Accessible tabs: click, or use the arrow keys, Home and End.
  - The chosen character steps forward on a podium under a spotlight, and the page accent changes to its colour.
  - A sample setup types out in a terminal, three status lights come on, then a chat question and answer appear. All of it is labelled "Illustrative sample".
- **Pinned scroll story.** Five chapters, scrubbed by scroll:
  1. An idea.
  2. The server materialises.
  3. The agents move in.
  4. A night sweep with the moon, an asleep laptop and a sample log.
  5. A glowing shell around the VM with blocked pings.
- **The rack** replaces the template cards: pull-out rack units with LEDs, a peeking character, honest status chips, the suggested plan and deploy links.
- **Handshake showpiece.** A token card, packets, five steps that check off, a budget meter (the real Standard price against a clearly labelled example cap) and a server that materialises and goes "online". It is flagged "Coming soon: Planned API, shown as a preview."
- **Plans as server blades** using real `db.plan` data and real deploy links. The FAQ is restyled, and the finale keeps "Your server is 47 seconds away."
- **Craft details:**
  - a gradient line that draws itself down the whole page with a glowing head
  - a cursor spotlight and grain
  - a bolder display type scale with kinetic headline reveals, and micro-lifts on buttons and cards
  - a Konami-code party and a startle when you scroll fast
  - a fixed "Pause animations" control that freezes CSS, Web Animations and SMIL animations
  - every section pauses when off screen
  - a reduced-motion version that is designed, not just switched off: everyone shown online, the story unpinned in its final state, the night shift shown finished
- **Brand-mark slots (your logo decision).**
  - `app/nxm/_data/ai-agents-marks.ts` maps each agent to `public/brand/agents/{openclaw,grok,claude,mcp,n8n}.svg`. The folder is empty apart from a `.gitkeep`.
  - When a file is present, the official mark shows as a small "runs …" mark beside the character, with its attribution line. Otherwise a text wordmark shows.
  - No logos were drawn, traced or scraped. With the wordmarks, the page looks complete.

### Screenshots and filmstrips
All in `/root/agent-notes/agents-marketing/v2/`:
- **Filmstrips:**
  - `film-hero-1440.png` / `film-hero-390.png`
  - `film-night-shift-beats-1440.png` / `film-night-shift-beats-390.png` (the beats, counter going 0 to 6)

For night shift, I'm planning to make it bigger and brighter: larger avatars and cards, bigger text, a brighter palette, stronger glow on the active agent, bigger particle bursts with a shockwave ring, a visible queue column with labeled chips, a "Done" tray where completed cards land, and a bigger beat indicator with the active beat highlighted.

To avoid flashing concerns, I need to rate-limit bursts so completions never exceed roughly 3 per second — I'll enforce a global minimum interval of about 400ms between bursts even if work durations overlap.

On mobile, I'm picturing a vertical flow: a queue stack at top, cards flowing down a spine to stacked agent rows, ending in a Done tray with a counter at the bottom.

I'm reworking the layout so the core/queue block becomes a static visible section on mobile (not absolutely positioned), adding a new done-tray element visible at all widths, and switching avatars to use SVG `<use>` symbols referencing shared defs for cleaner animated avatar instances.

Thinking about whether CSS animations defined on symbol content actually run inside `<use>` shadow instances — I recall Chrome and Firefox both support this since the selectors match the original symbol elements, though state classes toggled on the outer `<svg>` won't cross into the shadow tree to affect them.

This creates a problem for pause controls: a `.is-off` class on the root won't reach the use-instance shadow trees, so animations would keep running even when paused or offscreen, which is a minor performance concern but not something that breaks functionality — the symbol definitions live inside the defs block which is part of the root document, so I need to think about whether pause rules can target that instead.

The simplest fix is probably to just make the symbol instances static entirely, disabling their animations with a blanket override, since idle motion isn't critical for rack, blades, or tabs given their small size.

I can shift the hop motion from the inner avatar body to the whole SVG transform instead, letting that work with `<use>` just fine and sidestepping the paused/offscreen complexity. Tallying it up: hero, crew podium, night shift, story poses, and handshake still need inline SVG for state-dependent animation, while tabs, rack, blades, and final cast can all become `<use>` references — cutting inline instances roughly in half, which I should verify against gzip size before and after.

I'm worried about symbol definitions carrying animation classes like `.av-body` — if I put static art inside a shared symbol, I need to make sure CSS animations don't leak into cloned instances. I'm considering scoping a rule that disables animation/transition on everything inside the defs container, but I'm unsure whether `<use>` clones are style-matched as if they're the original element or isolated in a shadow tree, which determines whether that selector actually reaches them.

For the parallax story section, I'm planning layered background racks moving at different speeds and drawn-on connection lines using stroke-dashoffset tied to a scroll variable — even though that's technically outside my "transform/opacity only" rule for keyframes, I think it's an acceptable small exception since it's not using actual keyframe animations.

Adding gradient shading and rim light...

I also want secondary motion like antenna follow-through with delayed keyframes, squash-and-stretch on landings, and a couple extra expressions like sleepy eyelids.

Adding focus/wink expression classes...

 *  expressions, working states). With `label` it is announced; without, decorative. */
export function avatarSvg(id: CastId, label?: string): string {
  const a11y = label ? `role="img" aria-label="${label.replace(/&/g, "&").replace(/"/g, """)}"` : `aria-hidden="true" focusable="false"`;
  return `<svg class="av av-${id}" viewBox="0 0 160 160" ${a11y}>${ART[id]}</svg>`;
}

 *  motion or eye tracking): rack, plan blades, tabs, finale. */

}

I'm comparing the gzip sizes between v2 and the current version—raw size dropped by about 47KB, but gzip didn't shrink as expected since the symbol definitions are duplicating artwork across multiple defs instead of consolidating it.

The honest takeaway is raw HTML shrank 6% but gzip grew 3% because v3's richer art (shading, expressions) added genuinely unique content that doesn't compress as cheaply as repeated shapes. To actually reduce size further I'd need to look at which sections could reuse symbols instead of inlining—story and crew podium need inline markup for expressions and eye-tracking, but the hs Bit element could switch to a reusable reference to shave off one duplicate.

A better architectural fix occurs to me: instead of inlining avatar art everywhere in HTML, I could keep only the symbol definitions in the markup and have JS clone them into live SVGs wherever animation or eye-tracking is needed (hero, work, crew, story). That would drop the inline avatar count in the HTML to zero while still working without JS since the static copies render fine as a fallback—though I need to think through how to avoid an SSR flash before hydration kicks in.

I'll add an `avatarLive(id)` helper that outputs a placeholder svg with a `data-live` use reference, swap the loader to use it for avatar slots, keep `avatarSvg` exported for tests, and make sure hydration runs at the very top of page.js before anything queries pupil elements for tracking.

These numbers are rough given the shared, unaccelerated environment, but 5-14 fps at 4x throttle is still concerning. I should measure an unthrottled baseline and compare against a reference page under the same conditions to calibrate, then hunt for hotspots—likely culprits are drop-shadow filters on many SVGs, which are costly to raster in software especially with animated content inside filtered elements.

I'm suspecting the real bottlenecks are the full-screen fixed grain overlay using mix-blend-mode overlay (forcing a blend pass over the entire viewport every frame), the animated 70px blur on the aurora element, backdrop-filter on many cards, and drop-shadow filters on animated avatars. My optimization plan: swap the grain overlay to a normal-blend low-opacity noise texture (or disable on mobile), and replace the CSS drop-shadow filters on animated avatar elements with a static shadow ellipse instead, since filtering combined with transforms forces expensive repaints unless promoted to a compositor layer.

I'm also adding will-change: transform to parallax and aurora layers so their filters get rasterized once and the GPU can just transform the cached texture rather than recomputing it every frame, and stripping backdrop-filter off cards whose backgrounds are already nearly opaque since it's redundant there. The pupil-tracking code looks like it's causing layout thrashing too — it writes a transform then immediately reads getBoundingClientRect for the next avatar, forcing a forced synchronous layout each time, so I need to batch all the reads before any writes.

For the SVG animations, since SVG elements repaint the whole document on every animated frame rather than compositing individually, I'm considering an adaptive quality mode: measure the first 60 frames, and if the average frame time exceeds 24ms, switch to a "lite" mode that disables grain, spotlight, particles, and aurora rotation while keeping only the simplest breathing/blinking animations. I think the right next step is to implement these optimizations first, then benchmark unthrottled and throttled numbers to see how much they actually help.

Frame rate under 4x throttling is poor (5–14 fps on heavy sections). I'll calibrate against an existing page, then fix the hot spots—layout thrash in eye tracking, filters, and blend layers—and add an adaptive lite mode.

content.thinking:
Style recalc is eating 3.2 of 4 seconds, which points to repeated full-page recalculations — maybe something setting CSS custom properties on root or a clock/timer interval triggering constant style invalidation. I'm also seeing TimerFire at 1.3s, likely from a setInterval tied to animated face elements.

I'm checking which polling loops run at night: a wait() loop on an eye-glance interval every 2600ms writes transforms on tracked elements, while crew-select and handshake loops only fire when visible, so they're probably not the culprit on mobile night shift. The real cost might just be that the stylesheet is massive (262KB with tons of selectors), so even small class or custom-property toggles force expensive recalculation across the whole rule set.

The bigger suspect is that CSS animations running on SVG children are main-thread, not compositor, so each running animation forces an UpdateLayoutTree every frame — with many working avatars, rain, and spine animations simultaneously active, that cost multiplies under throttling. I want to check whether `.is-off` is actually pausing those animations at night, and count how many animations are genuinely running via `document.getAnimations()` to see what's active per section at that moment.

I'm noticing animation packets keep running even when their container is scrolled offscreen, so I need to add visibility tracking that pauses and resumes these in-flight animations rather than letting them burn cycles unseen. I also realize story animations continue playing while the user is viewing the crew section, which is another leak I need to address.

For the night shift view with 91 active animations plus 17 CSS transitions, the bottleneck seems to be style recalculation from main-thread SVG animations compounded by the throttling. I'm considering trimming effects on mobile—dropping the glyph rain, slowing ring spins—since each working avatar currently drives around five inner animations, adding up to roughly thirty concurrent main-thread animations just from the six avatars.

I'm also suspecting the heavy universal descendant selectors with !important (like the ones pausing animations on offscreen or paused containers) might be making style invalidation more expensive than necessary when a class toggles higher up the tree.

Toggling custom properties like `--night` or `.hot` on a container triggers a full subtree recalculation across thousands of nodes including SVGs, which is costlier than toggling a small list item class. At 4x throttling, the 3.2 seconds of layout cost over a 4-second window translates to roughly 20% real CPU usage on a mid-tier phone, so my plan is to keep outer composited effects like breathing and ring spin but disable inner SVG animations on mobile for avatars that aren't actively highlighted, preserving some visible motion without the full cost.

I also want to remove the glyph rain on mobile, pause offscreen packets, scope `--night` and `.hot` toggles to smaller targets like `.wk-sky` and `.wk-net` instead of the whole box, and account for the fact that pupil-tracking transitions still force per-SVG repaints during mouse movement across the hero — I'll note that tradeoff and move forward with implementing these fixes before re-measuring performance.

content.thinking:
I'm spotting a :root:has() selector in globals.css that's loaded portal-wide, including marketing pages — this matches a past lesson that scoping CSS this way triggers full-page restyle storms, since any DOM mutation anywhere could invalidate the :has match and force Chrome to recalculate styles broadly.

Checking which mutations trigger this: class attribute changes are narrowly invalidated, but DOM insertions (like setting innerHTML or textContent, which replaces a text node) trigger full-document invalidation. My log, counter, and clock updates all use textContent, which counts as insertion — I can't touch the portal CSS itself, but I can avoid this by mutating `firstChild.data` directly instead of reassigning textContent, since that's a characterData change rather than a node insertion.

I'm writing a setText helper that updates an existing text node's data when possible, falling back to textContent otherwise, and applying it to clock, counter, and live-region elements. I also realize the crew terminal's typing effect rewrites innerHTML on every keystroke, causing repeated full recalcs and explaining the mobile slowdown there — I need to restructure it so each line is a persistent span with a text node whose data gets extended as characters are typed, rather than regenerating HTML each time.

The cursor can stay as an appended span since it only moves once per line. Story and hero sections don't need changes since they're either static or use class toggles only. I'll also note in the report that the global `:root:has()` rule in app/globals.css triggers full-page restyles on any DOM insertion site-wide — a known hazard worth flagging to the owner, even though it's outside this portal's scope.

content.thinking:
I'm realizing the breathing animation on the inline SVG root isn't getting composited, which forces main-thread work. The fix is to move the transform animation onto the surrounding HTML wrapper elements instead, since those composite properly.

But .w-ch already uses inline JS-set transforms for parallax, so I need to animate the `scale` property separately rather than `transform` to avoid conflicts — Chrome composites individual transform properties like scale independently. So I'll drop the breathing animation off `.av` and instead apply a new scale-based keyframe animation to the wrapper elements, keeping transform-origin at the bottom for a natural squash effect.

I also need to make sure `.w-ch`'s existing drop-in animation on load stacks with the new breathing animation using multiple animation-delay values, and handle the hover-hop and party-mode one-off animations on the svg itself without conflict, plus update the lite mode selector to target the new wrapper classes instead of `.av`.

## /ai-agents v3 polish pass: done, with the two stale-copy fixes

All eight items and both copy bugs are done in commit `226e984d19` on branch `feature/ai-agents-hosting` (worktree `/tank/nxeon-wt-agents`). Nothing is merged or deployed. Typecheck is 0. The full suite matches main's 43 failures; one extra timing flake (`directory-blocklist`) passes 16/16 when run alone. The page test is now 10/10.

**What changed, in your order**
1. **Note vs pause button.** The pause button is no longer fixed on screen. It sits inline in the hero next to the note. On phones the note moves below the scene. Nothing overlaps at 1440, 820 or 390.
2. **Night shift.**
   - Bigger and easier to read: avatars up to 140px, cards up to 230px, text 0.9–1.1rem in lighter colours, brighter connection lines.
   - Clearer beats: numbered and highlighted (Queue → Dispatch → Work → Done), with a queue counter.
   - The working agent gets a strong glow and halo; finished cards fly into a new Done tray.
   - Completion bursts have 18 particles plus a shockwave ring, spaced at least 420ms apart, so under 3 flashes per second. Pause still works.
3. **Phone night shift** is now its own vertical flow: queue card at the top, a spine with travelling packets, agent rows, the Done tray and the counter.
4. **Page weight.** Each character's art now ships once as a shared SVG symbol.
   - Static spots (rack, plan blades, tabs, finale) use `<use>` copies.
   - Animated spots start as `<use>` and become inline copies in the browser, so the HTML carries no full copies.
   - Same dev server, before → after:

     | Measure | v2 | v3 |
     |---|---|---|
     | Raw HTML | 759,106 B | 557,868 B |
     | gzip -9 | 86,112 B | 80,428 B |
     | As served | 106,913 B | 99,032 B |

   - That's despite the richer character art. For reference, `/vibe-coding` is 387 KB raw / 57 KB gzip.
5. **Story** is down from 520vh to 350vh. It now has parallax rack and floor layers, wires that draw on as you scroll, and a pose per chapter: thinking, wow, landing squash, working at night, relieved.
6. **Character craft.**
   - Shading on every character: highlight, core shadow, cool rim light.
   - Follow-through on antennae, eye stalks and plug prongs, plus a squash-and-stretch landing.
   - Four expressions: happy, wow, focus, sleepy. The crew stage plays sleepy → wow → focus → happy as each agent boots. Night-shift workers wear focus while working.
7. **Accessibility** (Playwright script):
   - headings: no skipped levels
   - 9 labelled regions
   - contrast: 210 text elements checked, none below AA; approximate, since gradient backgrounds are treated as the nearest solid colour
   - live regions: polite; the night-shift summary is limited to one every 12s
   - focus order: hero buttons → Pause → night-shift Pause → crew tabs (arrow keys, Home/End) → panel
   - reduced motion: 0 running animations, static characters, the story is unpinned
8. **Frame rate at 4x CPU throttle.** Headless browser with software rendering on this shared box, load average 4–7; `/vibe-coding` holds 60fps under the same conditions. Two runs each:

   | Section | 1440 before | 1440 after | 390 before | 390 after |
   |---|---|---|---|---|
   | Hero | 9 | 32–51 | 24 | 24–29 |
   | Night shift | 11.5 | 33–34 | 5.6 | 23–35 |
   | Crew | 14 | 38–47 | 8.7 | 35–52 |
   | Story | 14 | 38–44 | 6.9 | 32–55 |
   | Rack | — | 44–54 | — | 57–58 |

   - Fixes behind the gains:
     - no CSS filters on animated layers
     - eye tracking no longer forces repeated layout
     - breathing runs on the outer wrapper, inner moves are periodic or only while active
     - packets are small dots on paths instead of animating a big SVG
     - the night shift reuses pooled elements and updates text in place
   - An automatic "lite" mode turns off grain, spotlight, particles and inner character motion on slow devices, or when the browser's Save-Data setting is on.

**Copy fixes**
- `/openclaw-vps-hosting` now says Node 24.16+ / 26.1+ (it said 22).
- `/n8n-hosting` drops every one-click claim, including the title. It now says to deploy with the Docker add-on and run n8n's official image, with a one-click template "coming soon".
- Both are covered by unit tests on the page builders. I couldn't render those two pages locally because the throwaway DB has no region rows, so the loader stops.

**Screenshots and filmstrips:** `/root/agent-notes/agents-marketing/v3/`, 27 files.
- Filmstrips per width (1440, 820, 390): hero, night shift, crew, story, handshake.
- `rack-plans-faq-*`, `full-*` and `full-reduced-motion-*` at each width.
- `hero-*` close-ups.

**Preview:** run `/tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/agents/dev.sh` and open http://localhost:3141/nxm/ai-agents. It uses the throwaway DB `nxeon_agt_agents`; cleanup steps are in the notes. Notes are in `/root/agent-notes/agents-marketing.md`.

**Still placeholder:**
- Prices in the screenshots are seed prices.
- No official logo files are in place; the attribution lines are placeholders the owner must replace per each project's brand rules.
- Everything marked "Coming soon" is still unbuilt.

**One finding outside this page:** the portal stylesheet `app/globals.css` uses `:root:has(.nx-shell-root)` rules. These make any page that adds DOM nodes recalculate styles for the whole document (about 6,200 elements each time). That was the main cause of the phone slowdowns, and it affects the whole site. I worked around it here, but the fix belongs in the portal CSS. I tried to file it as a background task but the call timed out, so it is not filed. This needs owner sign-off because it touches portal CSS.

**Honest self-critique**
- **Frame rate.** Still not a guaranteed 60fps on slow phones. The phone hero holds about 24–29fps and the night shift 23–35 under 4x throttling. The remaining cost is the character parts animating inside the SVGs (turning them off gives about 53fps). These numbers come from a noisy shared box without a GPU, not a real device.
- **Story.** The drawn-on wires are faint, and the poses switch per chapter rather than blending.
- **Night shift.** At 820 it falls back to the phone layout. A two-column tablet layout would use the space better.
- **Character craft.** The shading and expressions are a clear step up, but it is still programmer art. An illustrator pass would make the biggest difference to "legendary".
- **Contrast check.** It approximates gradient backgrounds, and I didn't do a real screen-reader run.

The v3 polish pass is done: all eight items, plus fixes for the stale OpenClaw and n8n copy. It's committed as `226e984d19` on `feature/ai-agents-hosting`, not merged or deployed. Typecheck has 0 errors, the page's tests pass 10/10, and the full suite shows the same 43 failures as main. One extra failure is the known timing flake, which passes when run alone.

**What changed:**
1. **Note vs pause button:** the pause button is no longer fixed on screen. It sits in the hero next to the note, and on phones the note moves below the scene. Nothing overlaps at 1440, 820 or 390.
2. **Night shift:**
   - Larger characters and cards, with bigger, higher-contrast text.
   - A strong glow on the working agent.
   - Bigger completion bursts with a shockwave ring.
   - A visible Queue → Dispatch → Work → Done flow ending in a "Done" tray.
   - Bursts are spaced at least 420 ms apart, so it stays under 3 flashes a second.
3. **Phone night shift:** its own vertical layout. The queue sits at the top, with a line carrying data dots down past each agent row, then the Done tray and counter.
4. **Page weight:** each character's art now ships once and is reused, instead of being pasted in about 49 times. On the dev server it went from 759 KB to 558 KB raw and from 107 KB to 99 KB as served, even with the richer art.
5. **Story:** shortened from 520vh to 350vh. It now has parallax background layers, wires that draw on as you scroll, and a new pose for the characters in each chapter.
6. **Characters:** shading and rim light, follow-through on antennas and claws, a squash-and-stretch landing, and four expressions (happy, wow, focus, sleepy).
7. **Accessibility:**
   - Headings and landmarks: no skipped heading levels, and every section is labelled.
   - Contrast: none of 210 text elements checked fell below the WCAG AA contrast ratio. The check approximates gradient backgrounds.
   - Activity feed: its screen-reader summary is polite and limited to one every 12 seconds.
   - Focus order: runs hero buttons → Pause → crew tabs (arrow keys work).
   - Reduced motion: shows a fully static page.
8. **Frame rate at 4x CPU throttling:** measured on this shared, GPU-less box, where the existing `/vibe-coding` page holds 60fps.

| Section | Before (1440 / 390) | After (1440 / 390) |
|---|---|---|
| Hero | 9 / 24 | 32–51 / 24–29 |
| Night shift | 11.5 / 5.6 | 33–34 / 23–35 |
| Crew | 14 / 8.7 | 38–47 / 35–52 |
| Story | 14 / 6.9 | 38–44 / 32–55 |

The main fixes were removing CSS filters from animated layers, stopping layout thrash in the eye tracking, and pooling elements in the night shift. The page also switches to a lighter mode automatically on slow devices.

**Copy fixes:** `/openclaw-vps-hosting` now says Node 24.16+ / 26.1+ instead of 22. `/n8n-hosting` drops every one-click claim, including in the title. It now says to use the Docker add-on with n8n's official image, with a one-click template "coming soon". I couldn't render those two pages locally because the test database has no regions, so they're checked by unit tests on the page content instead.

**One issue outside this page:** the portal stylesheet `app/globals.css` has rules that make the whole page recalculate its styles whenever content changes. That was the main cause of the phone slowdowns, and it affects every page on the site. I worked around it here, but the fix belongs in the portal CSS and needs the owner's sign-off. I tried to file it as a separate task but the call timed out, so it isn't filed.

**Still placeholder:** prices in the screenshots are seed prices, no official logo files are in place, and everything marked "Coming soon" is still unbuilt.

**Self-critique:**
- **Frame rate:** still not a guaranteed 60fps on slow phones. Most of the remaining cost is the moving parts inside the characters, and these are readings from a noisy shared box, not a real device.
- **Story:** the drawn-on wires are faint, and poses switch per chapter rather than blending.
- **Tablet:** at 820 the night shift uses the phone layout; a two-column tablet layout would use the space better.
- **Characters:** still programmer art. An illustrator pass would do the most to get this to "legendary".
